subtopic: INCENTIVES TO INCREASE PRODUCTIVITY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
INCENTIVES TO INCREASE PRODUCTIVITY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to move a motion, under Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In order to overcome our trade deficit of $12.5 billion a year in fully manufactured products, the ones which produce jobs, we must improve our productivity. To do so, we must offer incentives which will persuade producers that they will be able to pay for the new plant, machinery and production systems they will have to buy in a reasonably short space of time and in this way make it as easy as possible for them to make the usually high expenditures involved.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski):
That the government allow, first, that all capital expenditures involved in improving productivity be written off in one year; and, second, that a plant be rewarded in the form of a generous cash bonus at the end of the year in direct proportion to its increase in productivity during the year.

I refer to the fact that presumably under the minister's guidance the Bank of Canada is now taking steps to increase further interest rates in Canada.
Would the minister indicate and try to justify to the House why he feels higher interest rates are warranted, bearing in mind that for every half-point he bumps up the rates in the country it is costing the average home owner, over the life of his mortgage, $5,000 and in the aggregate it is costing businessmen, for every half-point increase, $375 million. Mr. Speaker, Bank of Canada policies are announced regularly when there are changes in interest rates. The Bank of Canada has not changed its rates lately, they are the same as before and the prime rate at Canadian banks is exactly the same as last month. As for the short term market fluctuations, the Bank of Canada has to take action from time to time, but that has no effect on interest rates for people usually borrowing on the market.

Mr. Speaker, surely the minister realizes it is not just a question of the Bank of Canada tampering with the bank rate: it has intervened in the sense of selling treasury bills with the deliberate purpose of raising short-term rates in the country. The government has stated publicly that the reason it is doing so is to somehow or other put our interest rate structure in better balance with U.S. interest rates.
Can the minister tell us, if we have a floating dollar as he has assured us we do, why he is still worried about the interest rate level domestically in Canada as compared with that in the United States?

I have said many times that the interventions of the bank are to make sure that fluctuations of the Canadian dollar take place in an orderly way. It is very important for Canadians to maintain a competitive level of interest rates with the United States if we are not to see an outflow of capital from Canada to the United States.

Once again, the Minister of Finance has carefully avoided dealing with the heart of the problem, that is, the current account deficit. It is absolutely foolhardy to be adjusting our interest rate structure and to be borrowing further capital funds such as the minister is hinting at if we permit the current account deficit to continue. I think the hon. member would realize, if he read the information that is public, that in 1978 we will have in Canada a record surplus in trade. In fact, in the first three quarters of the year the current account deficit was $200 million less than last year.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this motion indicates that there is unanimous support in the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments and the report deals particularly with the flagrant abuse of regulatory power by officials of the Department of Transport. On several occasions this committee has brought before the House reports in connection with our responsibility for examining the extent to which the power which this House and parliament gives to government, government officials and government agencies to act by order in council and regulation has been abused.
The extent of this can be shown by the fact that since our committee came into existence we have examined over 3,000 orders in council. Those are only orders in council which are not hidden, because a large number are not published. There are also directives and decrees which are not made public. It is fair to say that in the last three or four years there have been probably many thousand more than the 3,000 directives which I have mentioned affecting the people of this country, their lives, their property and their social problems, directives which have been prepared by bureaucrats, signed by ministers and have become the law of the land. Of those 3,000, we have said in respect of 1,200 cases that they should be challenged, objected to or queried. So when I say to the House that this is a considerable problem, Your Honour will be quite aware that I am not exaggerating.
The particular issue in question arose from an attempt by officials of the Department of Transport to deal with land adjacent to a number of airports in Canada. Those airports have been listed in the appropriate orders in council and cover St. Hubert, Calgary, Resolute Bay, Toronto international airport, Windsor, Sault Ste. Marie, Sarnia, Ottawa, North Bay, Hamilton, Kelowna, Sept- lies and Charlo airports. It is an order in council by which the minister, through his regulations, is given the power to send his agents or contractors to an adjacent property to cut down articles of natural growth, trees or what have you, and have them hauled away or disposed of as he sees fit.
In the first instance, this is far outside the terms of the enabling section in the statute. The pertinent section of the statute is section 6(1)(/') of the Aeronautics Act, which provides that the governor in council may pass regulations dealing with such things as regulations restricting, regulating or prohibiting the doing of anything or the suffering of anything to be done on any such lands-that is, lands adjacent to an airport. That is a very reasonable power to be given, but it is far less than the tremendous power given here by some official in the form of an order in council put before the governor in council to sign. I doubt very much that the cabinet examines too closely some of the orders in council they do sign, having in mind what I have read about them. The officials are empow-

December 13, 1978
Regulations
ered to go on the land and remove these articles and commodities of natural growth.
This particular order in council is covered in clause 7 of the regulations gazetted in 1978. It reads:
Where an owner or occupier referred to in section 6 permits an object of natural growth to exceed in elevation any of the surfaces set out.. . the minister may make a direction that any person may enter upon the land on which the object is growing and remove the excessive growth thereof.
If this parliament, which all too frequently is careless about the power it gives to the governor in council or to ministers to exercise authority by order in council, wishes that this be done, then let the government come to parliament and seek that power. Let us not leave it to some unknown, unnamed, faceless bureaucrat to make this particular regulation.
I suggest that in substance this authority may not be as much as some hon. members might feel it should be, but to me and to anyone who prizes parliamentary government in this country it seems we should stop and ask ourselves how far we are prepared to go to give authority to governments, to government departments and to government agencies to act by order in council without in any way examining the extent to which use is made of that power.
On several occasions our committee has made representations to the House, we have brought in reports to the House, but they have been ignored and neglected, and it is a matter of considerable importance that the Prime Minister, at the federal-provincial conference of February of this year, proposed that some steps should be taken to examine the growth of the regulatory power to see what should be done to curtail it.
In a letter of July of this year the Prime Minister wrote to the president of the Economic Council of Canada, Dr. Ostry, for whom I have considerable admiration, but in this case the letter was late, probably too little and too late. Dr. Ostry and her advisers only had between July and November of this year to make an interim report. The interim report went some distance along the road, but asking bureaucrats, who are probably members of the task force, or other bureaucrats in government to look at the problem of too much regulatory power is like asking rats to make the rat trap in which they will be forced to put themselves some time in the future. I am speaking figuratively, of course.
The Prime Minister is thoroughly familiar with rats, of course, and I do not feel that what I am saying is unknown to him in that respect. But 1 point out, Mr. Speaker, that if any body or any forum is going to exercise the care and scrutiny which there should be in respect of a matter of this kind, it is this House and this parliament. We have been careless and slovenly in the extent to which we have given away these powers and in our failure to ride herd on what happens to them after we have given them away. The Prime Minister recognized that, I think. He would make a great man in opposition. If he were in opposition, he would make a great rebel. When he is in power, of course, he believes in exercising all the authority on which he can lay his hands. When the devil is ill, the devil an angel would be; when the devil is well, the devil an angel is he. That is the way I think of the Prime Minister.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak very briefly to the motion of concurrence in the report. I do so in order officially to apprise the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments of an order in council which was the subject of a question of privilege brought before the House last Friday. I am referring to order in council No. PC 1978-3243 of October 26, 1978 which was proclaimed in the Canada Gazette on November 8.
The reason it was the subject of a question of privilege before the House was that the order in council proclaimed on November 8 enacts or proclaims into law a clause of a bill which is still before the House, namely, clause 2 of Bill C-14. Mr. Speaker intervened during the course of the question of privilege and suggested that in the normal course of the work of the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments this matter would come before it. Also Mr. Speaker suggested that the question of privilege could be disposed of by referring it to the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments without prejudice to any question of privilege which may arise from it.
My reasons for participating in this motion are twofold. First, I should like to apprise the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments of the importance of dealing with this matter as soon as possible because Bill C-14 has not been disposed of. It has not had third reading; it is still before committee. Also, I do so because of the tremendous backlog of work facing the committee. According to the committee report, it has considered 3,047 regulations. It has objected to, queried and requested explanation, including matters raised by counsel prior to submission of an instrument to the committee with explanation attached, of 1,125 statutory instruments or regulations.
Regulations
In the normal course of events, the committee would not deal with this particular regulation or statutory instrument, passed by cabinet in October and proclaimed in the Canada Gazette in November, for some time. It would be considerably after the House gave third reading to Bill C-14 and it passed the other place. That represents the quandary embodied in my intervention.
Before Bill C-14 is passed by parliament, the committee should rule as to whether government had the authority to enact that order in council which embodies the provisions of clause 2 of Bill C-14. If the government did not have that statutory authority, it is in contempt of the House and it would be the legitimate subject of a question of privilege. On the other hand, if the government had the statutory authority to enact the provisions of clause 2 of Bill C-14, then why did it bother to ask parliament to pass clause 2 or why did the government bother to include clause 2 in Bill C-14?
In conclusion, I congratulate the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) and his co-chairman, Senator Forsey, on the excellent work which the committee has been doing as the watchdog of parliament's rights respecting legislation and the power or practice of the government to go beyond legislation all too often by enacting regulations flowing from legislation. I should like to apprise him, his co-chairman and the members of the committee of the urgency of giving consideration to order in council No. PC 1978-3243 passed on October 26. I say this because of its conflict with Bill C-14, and because it may very well put the government in contempt of parliament, which would be a legitimate subject of a question of privilege in the House.

Mr. Speaker, I too want briefly to enter the debate on this particular motion and to join with those who have already spoken in support of the proposition we have before us; that is to say, putting into place a procedure which I think will very much improve the effectiveness of the operations of the Joint Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments. That committee is doing yeoman service not only on behalf of members of this House but on behalf of the people of Canada, looking as it does at the incredible number of regulations that we see in government today and that affect very seriously the lives of people across the country.
I could not help but note that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) in his interjection referred to the fact that this government has introduced a provision in law which allows for the establishment of this committee and allows the committee to look at regulations from time to time. As I recall, this was brought forward on a motion by Mr. John Turner, who is known to the Prime Minister, I think, when he was minister of justice.
I want also to point out the fact that while this move on the part of the government was extremely worth-while, and we in fact want to give credit where credit is due, we do go through a process of evolution in the considerations of this committee, learning from our experience in dealing with various regulations, statutory instruments and a variety of orders in council.
My hon. friend from St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) has pointed out an example of the kind of consideration we might now give in respect of legislation before the House. This is a matter of very considerable importance when there appears on the face of it to be conflict between a regulation which in fact has been passed or proclaimed by order in council and a section of a bill being considered by a standing committee of this House.
I simply want to say that in my estimation we should try to broaden the operations of this committee in the interests of the people we represent, because from time to time there are occasions when it is drawn to our attention as members of parliament that there are regulations in place, or potentialities in terms of legislation, which would have serious consequences in the form of regulatory control on the lives of the people of this country. Sometimes I have felt we have been somewhat constrained within the committee in dealing with these particular matters until they came up in a post mortem sense, as referred to by the hon. member for Peace River.
I want to give my full support and endorsation to that which has been said by those who have spoken already. This is another step in the attempt to come to terms with the evergrowing government by regulation with which we are faced these days. I hope the report will receive unanimous concurrence at this time.

I may have to step out of the House before hearing the opposition's point of view, but my colleague the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers (Mr. Andras) will stay throughout the debate and keep me very well informed.
We are talking about Canada's economic problems, and I know they have led to many questions about our future economic prospects. Even though we have created jobs at a record pace, unemployment is still too high; and even though we have managed to bring our domestic costs and prices under control, the lower value of the dollar and the rapid rise in prices for some food products continue to exert inflationary pressures.
Canadians are frustrated by the perception that a country as rich in human and natural resources as ours still is not realizing its economic potential. There is a strong sense that we must work together to strengthen the structure of industry in Canada, to develop our manufacturing, resource and service sectors in a manner that increases our international competitiveness and that allows the economic potential of each region to be realized.
Canadians have looked to the government for leadership and direction, and we have responded through a number of specific measures. It is important to recognize the principles that have guided our actions. We do not believe that governments alone can create a strong and healthy economy. Economic development and growth must be based on a competitive and dynamic private sector. This can be achieved only by the government and private sector acting together in ways that are mutually supportive.
The private sector must lead this process, but government support is necessary in three broad areas: first, to create a climate for growth to ensure that the general policies and programs of government support initiative, risk taking and innovation; second, to assist economic development directly where necessary and desired, to help the entrepreneur to take advantage of new opportunities to promote healthy, viable and dynamic regional economies to ease the burdens of adjustment for those individuals and regions where adjustment is required; and third, to assist in the provision of basic infrastructures that will enable the private sector to develop new initiatives and open up new markets.

The steps we took follow the principles 1 just mentioned and reinforce them. First of all, we are doing everything we can to ensure the recovery and the prosperity of the world economy. Trade being a vital necessity for Canada, we are taking an active part in international meetings to foster that world

December 13, 1978
Economic Development
recovery and prevent the escalation of protectionism which could jeopardize our economic well-being. I participated in four summit conferences, and particularly in Bonn, as leaders of major industrialised countries, we managed to take firm and decisive steps that will help bring back stability, growth and confidence.
We are actively pursuing the multilateral trade negotiations. We have specific interests to protect and promote as Canadians and we will continue firmly to assert them. At the same time, it is in our interest to fight protectionist policies which will hurt all countries, but particularly Canada.
Second, we have taken and will continue to take steps to create in Canada a healthy economic climate, a climate of confidence favourable to business growth and prosperity. Our anti-inflation program helped our industry regain its competitiveness in Canada and on world markets. We are also clearly determined to ensure that wage settlements in the public sector do not threaten to reduce that competitiveness by moving faster than in the private sector. We are also determined to reduce the part the government takes in economic activity and government interference in private sector decisions. We will continue to examine our social programs to ensure they provide sufficient assistance to those in need without reducing the incentive to work and the spirit of entrepreneurship. And if it is possible to improve on those programs, we will not hesitate to take the necessary steps, as we did recently in the case of family allowance payments and unemployment insurance benefits.
Finally, we took a certain number of specific steps to help Canadian industry:
-We have offered help and incentives to small businesses. We have reduced considerably their paperwork and decided to lower the excise tax and the capital gains tax.
-Changes to corporate income tax have helped industry to face the distortion in real benefits caused by inflation.
-We have increased help to Canadian exports through the Export Development Corporation. And, in co-operation with the private sector, we are setting up a last-risk insurance formula guaranteed by the government.
-We have started rationalizing our programs of direct help to manufacturing and processing industries by establishing the business assistance program. Regional committees were created in all provinces and are directed by representatives of the private sector. Through that program, we have improved adaptation and innovation spirit in Canadian industry. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) also announced recently that the funds available will be doubled next year and that the maximum guaranteed loans to the private sector will rise from $350 million up to $1 billion.
-We have sharply increased our help to research and development in Canada. We hope that expenses for research and development will amount to 1.5 per cent of our gross

national product within five years, particularly in the private sector, and we have offered major tax incentives to facilitate the pursuit of that objective. Even though it may vary from one industry to another and from one region to another, enterprises located in the maritimes can now get the equivalent of $1 in new research and development for every 150 to 200 they spend.
Research and development are necessary if we want to set up highly technical industries which will be able to compete on the international level in the 80's. However, research and development alone are not always enough. This is why the government took some action recently to provide direct assistance on the hand to the aerospatial industry to help develop the Challenger which already has had an amazing success and, on the other hand, to the communications industry to promote in Canada the commercial development of communications satellite techniques. This is also why we implemented recently a $400 million program to promote the commercial development of new industries in the field of renewable energy resources. This is also why we shall continue to look for opportunities to break through and means to be successful in various major sectors.
In the context of the new economic development objectives set at the end of last summer, we have announced new expenditures of approximately $450 million for next year. These funds will be used to support the achievement of our industrial development objectives, which include job creation, further training for Canadian workers, naval construction and repairs, as well as the establishment of an infrastructure to promote our raw material industries and our tourist industry.
Finally, in the last budget we announced important measures which will truly help us contain domestic costs after wage and price controls are phased out. At the same time, they will provide a more direct stimulus to economic growth by promoting investment and increasing the purchasing power of Canadians.
All of this has started to bring about some results. The number of jobs has gone up significantly since 381,000 new jobs were created between November, 1977, and November, 1978, including 123,000 in the manufacturing sector. Our trade balance is good and still improving. The use of our manufacturing capacity has expanded during the first half of this year and has now reached the usual level. Confidence is increasing.
Last February, the premiers endorsed the general principles of industrial and economic development I already mentioned. But we went further together. We developed a sophisticated consultation and review mechanism involving businesses as well as unions and governments. Working groups have been established to evaluate the present situation and the future prospects for 21 different manufacturing sectors as well as
December 13, 1978

tourism and construction. Those working groups have met with some 350 representatives from Canadian enterprises and more than 50 authorized union representatives, most of them presidents of affiliated unions. People from universities and the public service were also involved in that study. All those groups have produced reports and made a total of 850 recommendations on concrete measures.
All those reports have been submitted to the public and to a steering committee composed of five representatives from unions, five from businesses and one from the universities. The report of that steering committee was published last October 23. It includes a summary of sectorial reports and makes a number of specific recommendations.
The government committed itself to respond to that review of various industrial sectors and to give it a new thrust. A first series of response to the steering committee report has just been published. The premiers met two weeks ago to study the progress made and they have agreed that all governments should work very seriously in that respect. We also agreed on the success of consultations and the need to further them in a way acceptable to all parties concerned. However, I wish to express today my congratulations and thanks to all people who have been involved in those consultations. They have been of enormous service to the country, Mr. Speaker.

It is time, Mr. Speaker, to take the next step. We need to continue and strengthen the process that most recently resulted in the second tier exercise, and to ensure by policy decision that needed action is taken: action to influence the development of industries and regional economies to the benefit of all Canadians; action to integrate programs and activities providing direct support to industry in order to increase effectiveness and minimize red tape; and action to foster co-operative relationships with respect to industrial development with the provinces, with business and labour and with other public and private organizations.
To lead and concert these actions, I have proposed the creation of a new Board of Economic Development Ministers.
Under the leadership of its president, that board will be charged with: defining an integrated federal approach to the provision of direct support to industry and economic development in Canada, including government procurement policy, both by industrial sector and by region; it will be charged with reviewing and co-ordinating proposals by departments prior to their submission to cabinet or Treasury Board; and, finally, it will be charged with developing mechanisms to improve and to integrate program delivery at the local level.
The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Buchanan), who will sit as ex officio members of the Board of Economic Development Ministers, will provide that board and its president with essential counsel and support.
The other members of the board at the outset will be the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), the
Economic Development
Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard), the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell), the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Gillespie), and the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Abbott). Other ministers will sit in at meetings of the board that deal with matters affecting their responsibilities; the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc), the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), for example, would be amongst these.
1 should emphasize that individual ministers will continue to be responsible for the administration of their departmental programs, but their efforts in this area will be led and concerted by the new Minister of State for Economic Development. In addition to his role as President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers, that minister will: advise Treasury Board on the allocation of financial and other resources to programs that provide direct support to industry and economic development, including programs in the field of enterprise development, employment creation, regional expansion, resource industries and researcn and development; and he will lead and co-ordinate the efforts of the government to establish co-operative relationships with the provinces, business, labour and other groups to promote a healthy, dynamic and regionally balanced industrial sector.
The purpose of this reorganization is to focus and streamline our efforts in this area, to do more with what we have and to do it in a more co-ordinated and consistent way. To underline this, the budget and staff authority for the ministry of state will fall within the already announced budgetary and staff ceilings of the government, so that no new dollars or person-years will be required.
The economic measures we adopted in August are being implemented according to the principles we enunciated in October of 1976 in the white paper called "The Way Ahead". In that document we said:
Canada's economic prospects in the 1980's are matched by few other industrialized countries. Canada's opportunities for continued real growth lie in its relative wealth of resources, its abundant food producing potential, its technology, and, of course, its highly skilled and educated population. They lie, not least, in Canadians' capacity for enterprise. But to take advantage of these opportunities, to ensure that our substantial potential is indeed attained, Canadians and their governments will have to meet a number of major challenges.
I am confident that the Board of Economic Development Ministers, under the leadership of its president, will make a major contribution to meeting these challenges and, with the co-operation of all Canadians, will help to lay the foundation for a decade of prosperity in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the beginning I want to say to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that I understand other engagements will take him out of the House shortly. I appreciate his publicly drawing attention to that as his reason for having to be absent during a portion of my remarks, those of the leader of the New Demo-

December 13, 1978
Economic Development
cratic Party and others who may want to take part in this debate.
I should say to him also that we welcome him back from wherever he has been, and certainly on behalf of everyone in this House I want to assure him of our continued interest in whatever it is he will be doing.
First of all, I want to deal with the general problem of bringing some order to the management of government in an age that is growing more and more complex and it becomes more and more difficult for governments to bring some kind of coherence and direction to their affairs. There is no question that there is a very serious management problem that faces any kind of government. That problem is likely to continue being serious as the growth of government continues and as demands upon government become more complex.
In my judgment-and 1 think it is important that this be raised at the time of the creation of yet another layer of government activities by this administration-that natural problem that is associated with growth and complexity has been very seriously aggravated in Canada by the way in which this particular government has approached organizational problems. It has approached them by throwing aside for all practical purposes the traditional central instruments of policy decision in a country like Canada. There has been a virtual destruction of the cabinet of Canada as a source of policy. I am not going to comment on the other evidence of destruction in this particular cabinet. That is there for all to see.
What is important in institutional terms is that with previous governments under previous prime ministers it was clear that the place where policy decisions were taken was the cabinet room. It was clear that a C. D. Howe, a Jimmy Gardiner and other ministers of that era, and, indeed, ministers of the era in which the Prime Minister himself first came to Ottawa during the days of the Pearson government, were clearly people at whose desk the buck stopped. They were people who were called upon to make final decisions, who had power to summon information and who had direct access to the ear of the prime minister, and thus were in a position to act on that information.
That era is finished as far as this government is concerned. It is finished because of a deliberate attempt to move away from cabinet for motives which may well have been valid, although the experience over the last decade has shown that they were very badly considered. It was decided to move away from cabinet in the name of co-ordination and efficiency and to vest the power to decide in agencies other than the elected ministers of a government responsible here on the floor of this House of Commons. This, of course, has been accompanied by an excessive concentration of power in the hands of appointed bureaucrats in the Privy Council office and in the Prime Minister's office .
I should say in passing that this has been quite a new development in Canadian history. There is nothing new at all about public servants, senior public servants in particular,
[Mr. Clark.)
making decisions; that has always been the case. They have always had a heavy influence on decision-making. Some of us in the elected body of government think it is too heavy, but it is in the nature of things that those who come up through the public service should exercise an important influence on policy decisions in fields in which they have detailed, day to day knowledge. What is new is that this Prime Minister, in the interests of efficiency, put aside his cabinet as the central source of advice, and did not turn to the traditional public service, turning instead to a new group of public servants, by and large people chosen by himself and chosen with a purpose, one of the criteria being their ability to fit into his particular view of how government should be organized and what the country was.
We consequently saw the power over decisions move away from cabinet, its traditional source, move away from traditional public servants, and instead become concentrated in the Privy Council office and in the Prime Minister's office . That is an example of one thing that was done. I want to return later to some of the implications of that development as it pertains to the Canadian parliamentary system.
Another factor that is seriously aggravating the difficulty of governing in this country is the difficulty of getting decisions. One difficulty in the way of coherent policy has been excessive insistence on secrecy by the government opposite. My colleagues and I, along with members of parliament from other parties in this House, have made the point before that this is probably the most secretive of governments in the western world, it is not only Canadians at large who do not know what is going on in the government which their tax money pays for; it must be immensely difficult for ministers of the Crown, and indeed for the Prime Minister, to have any certain sense of what is going on in a government where a habit of secrecy has grown up, where a habit of keeping things away from people has grown up. People should know those facts because once you begin to shut out the wider world, the inevitable effect is to shut out the smaller world, no matter whether that is the cabinet, the Privy Council or the Prime Minister's office. They have to have information if they are going to make decisions that will be intelligent in the context of a complex and changing country.
A third action by this government which has seriously aggravated the very difficult problem of organizing to deal effectively with national policy has been the insistent and consistent restriction of the House of Commons, and the restriction of the ability of the House of Commons to hold government accountable. It remains a matter of grave concern to me, sir, and to others who have an interest in the system of parliamentary democracy, to know that one of the first acts by this government in relation to parliament-it was certainly the first thing that happened in their first year of office in 1969- was the imposition by closure of changes in the rules of this House of Commons which took away the power to control spending. By removing that power to control spending, it removed the power of this parliament to scrutinize what was going on in government. This consequently removed from the
December 13, 1978

ministers, from the public servants and from the appointed little elite in the Privy Council office and in the Prime Minister's office the constraint of knowing that what they might be doing was subject to challenge and question by members of parliament here in this House of Commons. That pattern was established very early in their regime.
By the way, sir, that was the first time in the history of British parliamentary tradition that closure was used to force a change in the rules of the House of Commons. This insistence on keeping parliament distant from its job, interfering with parliament's ability to control, to know what was going on and to hold government responsible, has been a part of the pattern and the approach of this government to parliament.
All of us speak most truly when we lose our tempers. When the Prime Minister lost his temper in this House some years ago and referred to members opposite as being mere nobodies when they were 50 yards from the House of Commons, he was expressing the view of parliament as an institution which has ever since informed this government that that is a view which is inconsistent with, and runs against, the very basic history and purpose of parliament from its earliest days. The refusal to let parliament play its role of holding the government responsible has seriously aggravated the already difficult problem of bringing coherence and direction to the management of government.
Along with others in this House I have often spoken on the subject of secrecy. We intend to open up the system by the introduction of a freedom of information bill along the lines proposed by my hon. friend, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). Recently on an allotted day we spoke about some of the changes we would want to see in parliamentary practice so as to restore to parliament the power to hold government responsible, the power for which parliament was created and the power which was taken away by this government as one of its very first acts.
Let me speak at a little more length about the role of cabinet traditionally in the Canadian parliamentary system, because there has not been much opportunity to do so in this House. I suppose there are two authorities to whom we can turn for testimony as to the change in the central role of cabinet. One source would be authors who have described the works of parliament and governments over the years in Canada, in Britain and in other systems which have the parliamentary tradition. From this particular source it will be found that the verdict is consistent, that it has always been the cabinet in which the power to decide was located and situated. But perhaps an even more eloquent expression of the change that has occurred in Canada under this government, a change that has involved making the cabinet of Canada insignificant, is offered by the practice of very many strong men who came to this House of Commons as members of parliament in the expectation that the tradition of cabinet as the place of power would continue, but who were forced to leave or who found themselves wanting to leave parliament when they found that the cabinet offices that they held had less influence than the particular portfolio had held a decade ago, or indeed that they

as elected ministers of the Crown had less influence on public policy events than members of small, appointed elites of friends in the Privy Council office and the Prime Minister's office .
The real testimony concerning the gutting of the Canadian cabinet as a place of decision comes from people like the Hon. John Turner, the Hon. Donald Macdonald and the Hon. Gerard Pelletier. The people who came to serve in a system where cabinet had power and the ministers had power found instead that they were serving in a system in which it was possible for the Prime Minister and his advisers, for example, to call in seven economic experts and locate them in the Privy Council or in the Prime Minister's office so they could second-guess the minister of finance on national budgetary policy.
That is a precise symbol of what happened under this government in regard to cabinet over the years and the result has been the gutting of the cabinet, the removal from cabinet of the power to establish national policy which, in common sense, has to be the only system within which the democratic, responsibly elected government can function. To put this in perspective, it might be interesting, sir, to-

It would be interesting to set on the record some of the figures of growth in the Privy Council office during the period in which it has become the centre of power in Canada, when the cabinet was gutted of the influence it has traditionally held through our system. In 1968 the number of persons permanently employed in the Privy Council office was 63; in 1977 it was 469. The total budget for the Privy Council office is up from $6.4 million in 1968 to $22.2 million in 1977.
One result has been a policy-making process so centralized and so cumbersome that many of the best ministers in the government, people who knew the tradition under which ministers had the power to decide, have quit in frustration. They have done so rather than try to work through the maze of this intermediary agency which has been put in to replace the traditional system of cabinet government.
It is interesting to note that during the same period the budget of the Prime Minister's office increased from $767,000 in 1968 to $2.7 million in the current year. One of the results of this growth has been a continuing isolation of the Prime Minister not only from his cabinet colleagues but also, sadly, from the people whose problems he and his government are here to respond to and resolve.
There is no question, as I said at the beginning, that some of the problems of organization of a government in difficult times

December 13, 1978
Economic Development
are complex in their nature. And there is no question that the structure presently in place for governing Canada at the federal government level is not working. Clearly there need to be changes made. It seems to me and to this party that there are some principles on which we should stand. One of those should be that ministers of the Crown, elected individuals sitting in and responsible to the Elouse of Commons, should set policy; that responsibility for setting policy, for making the final decisions, should not be cast off to some little elite sitting in isolation in the Privy Council office or the Prime Minister's office, but that it should be the ministers who carry the can. Indeed, one of the shocking things about the last two or three years in the House of Commons has been the frequency with which ministers have been prepared to chuck off to public servants the responsibility which should have properly been residing with ministers. They do that because they have become accustomed to being people through whose offices the buck passes rather than being people in whose offices the buck stops.
Another thing which is obviously important here is the capacity in the capital of Canada not only to set policy but to co-ordinate policy, to make sure, if I might draw some hypothetical examples, that one level of government is not proposing a policy of decentralization at the same time as another level of government is entering into extensive lease-purchase arrangements to buy new space in communities which public servants are being asked to leave. There needs to be some kind of co-ordination to ensure that the left hand of government- the large, left hand-knows what the right hand of government is doing. Clearly, this needs to be another of the principles which should be followed when considering the restructuring of government in this country as a means of trying to ensure that responsible politicians carry the burden of decision and assure co-ordinated direction to national policy.
Normally I would not talk about the internal preoccupations of opposition parties, but since this is a matter of some concern to us today, and since the problems of opposition will be a matter of continuing concern to the hon. members across the floor as soon as an election is called, I think it might be appropriate for me to make reference in passing to the fact that we in opposition, trying to do our job of keeping on top of what government is doing, have had to face some of those problems of organization ourselves and we have certainly taken a long, hard look at what is going wrong with the system which is in place now.
It became clear to us earlier this year that one of the things that is lacking in the Government of Canada-and, frankly, it was also lacking in our structure-was a capacity to co-ordinate the initiatives and the interest of members of parliament, whether ministers of the Crown or critics of ministers of the Crown, who have specific responsibilities. There has to be some means of bringing these different ministers and spokesmen together. For that reason we in the official opposition established the practice of appointing policy co-ordinators, the practice of establishing six broad fields-economic policy, social policy, cultural policy, policy relating to transport and

communications, food and resources, and policy relating to government operations.
I have designated a senior colleague in my caucus to serve as the co-ordinator, generally free of line responsibilities, so that he can draw together the activities of other spokesmen and put together a view of what was going on in relevant ministries and departments on the other side. This has worked reasonably well and, indeed, when I first heard the press release indicating the change which is the subject of our discussion today I thought that perhaps the government had borrowed yet another idea from us and was attempting to bring into its own structure that same process of co-ordination which we have pioneered here and which, by and large, has been a success in terms of the organization of our ability to meet our responsibilities. Without offence, I wish to say that this pertains only to parties in opposition which have enough members to organize, but I am sure the leader of the New Democratic Party will take at least an academic interest in what I have been saying.

My colleague, the hon. member for Peace River, suggests that the minister has been converted to metric. Let me deal for a moment with the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, because it is quite clear that if the new minister's responsibilities mean anything at all, they absolutely gut the mandate of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. They take away the basic role of that department. That is quite explicit. Because in describing the central role of the new minister, the Prime Minister says that it will be a role of formulating and developing new and comprehensive policies as well as of leading and co-ordinating the efforts of the Government of Canada to establish co-operative relationships with the provinces, business and labour.
That description of duties strikes right at the heart of the whole operation of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce last February to co-ordinate the 23 sectoral task
Economic Development
forces and to bring them together in a comprehensive package. That was the purpose of that program, which was the major program of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce at the time, and that purpose has been taken away holus-bolus, completely. That program is not to be co-ordinated; it is to be run, as nearly as we can make out from these terms of reference, by the new minister. So we have the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce standing with one foot in a swimming pool and the other foot in the metric system, with nothing else to hold on to or to administer.
Another department which has been very significantly changed-and I am sorry that the minister responsible had to leave the House temporarily-is the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. I say in passing that one of the failures we in this party most regret has been the failure of this government in relation to regional economic expansion. We remember, and will naturally ensure that the citizens of Atlantic Canada remember whenever an election is called, the undertaking by the Prime Minister to establish a kind of Marshall Plan for Atlantic Canada.
We remember his undertaking to solve the traditional problems of disparity. We know what has happened. We know that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has been an insignificant department. It has been up against the giants in this government. Every initiative it has taken has been undercut by other policies whether those policies were in the field of tariffs, which have continued discrimination against the Atlantic region, in the field of tax policy, which has failed to recognize the particular needs of that region, or in the field of concepts like "user-pay", which has deeply undercut any sensible prospect of development in Atlantic Canada. Nonetheless, the shell of the department remains.
There is a very real question as to what responsibilities the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion will have when the explicit mandate of the new super minister is to establish, and I quote:
-the most appropriate means by which the Government of Canada may . . . have a beneficial influence on the development of industries and regional economies in Canada-
What in the world is the mandate of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, if that is the mandate of the new super minister? I see that the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion has now returned to the House, after my having described how his department has disappeared and has been taken over by his colleague, the new super minister.
The third department which is quite significantly downgraded, it seems to us, is the Department of Finance. The Minister of Finance, for reasons on which I am sure the new minister will elaborate, is only an ex officio member of this new board. It is not exactly clear what that means or how that distinguishes him from other ministers. Perhaps it means that he has the right to say a quiet "no", whereas the others are expected to snap to attention whenever the super minister gives an order. As has been suggested, perhaps some sort of liaison is to be kept open between the Minister of Finance and the super minister, who is really responsible for establishing economic

policy in the country. However, there is no question at all that there has been a significant downgrading of the role, the power and the influence upon policy of the minister, the ministry and the Department of Finance in the country.

speechtext: As long as he doesn't take it.

subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
As I understand the provision here, the Minister of Finance is free to take actions in his field as minister, as long as they have no impact on economic development. It may well be that that is simply a description of what has been happening in Canada for the last two or three years, because there has been a minister of finance who has had singularly little positive impact upon economic development. This raises some very real questions as to what the continuing role of the Department of Finance and the Minister of Finance will be and whether any of their initiatives which would have an impact upon economic development in the country have to be cleared with some other minister. Just exactly what is the relationship here? Whatever it is, it is clear that the Minister of Finance and his department have been downgraded by the establishment of this new super ministry. The super minister's responsibility will be to do what all of us assumed the Department of Finance has been doing or has been responsible for doing.
I do not think it is clear exactly what the responsibilities of the new minister are in relation to the budget, but certainly on the off chance that this government's budget might have some positive impact on the economy, he would appear to have the obligation to vet that proposal in advance and he might very well have the power to veto proposals for a budget put forward by a minister of finance.
Once again the fourth ministry which, in our judgment, has been significantly downgraded is the Treasury Board. I say that with some regret because one of the causes of great difficulty with this government has been the degree to which the role of the Treasury Board has been diminished in recent years. There is now a provision in these terms of reference which empowers the new minister to advise the Treasury Board-it is not a question of "he may advise"; it is a question of "he shall advise", the Treasury Board-on the allocation of financial, personnel and other resources to federal programs that provide direct support to the development of economic enterprise in Canada.
It would seem to me that that term of reference takes a great deal of the raison d'etre of the traditional purpose of the Treasury Board away from the President of the Treasury Board and vests it in the new minister. What is he to be left with if he has to take advice which "shall be given" by the new minister? Of course, he would be left with approving LIP grants and one or two other matters, as well as his pay, but most of the important responsibilities that have an impact on the economic development of the country have been taken

away from the President of the Treasury Board and his department has been seriously downgraded.
The Department of Science and Technology, to which the Prime Minister made some reference in his remarks, has been virtually eliminated. Its shadow lingers on. It is attached to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, but its power is passed quite clearly to the new super minister who has the authority to initiate and co-ordinate research and development studies, to initiate proposals for new R and D policies, programs and activities, and to evaluate existing and proposed policies, programs and activities to ensure consistency with federal development policies, and to recommend changes therein.
The question to me is: If you are going to take away the powers of the Minister of State for Science and Technology, why not wipe out the department and have those powers exist in only one place in the government, namely, the new super ministry, rather than continuing the fiction that we have a super minister with those powers as well as a Minister of State for Science and Technology with those powers? It reminds me of the situation of the environment where we have two ministers doing one job. It makes very little sense in that case as it makes very little sense in this case.
I must say in passing, since the Prime Minister spoke glowingly about the importance of research and development to the Canadian economic future and about the priorities that his party and his government attach to research and development, that I would like to restate our view that one of the most serious mistakes that has been made by this government- which means it was serious indeed, because they have made a number that were dangerous to this country-was their deliberate decision to buy technology abroad. We are paying for that daily in the leakage out of this country of innovators and researchers, of people whose initiative could help make Canada competitive in the world. They are leaving the country because it was the deliberate policy of the government in the name of research and development to drive them away.
There are a few other matters of curiosity in relation to the ambit of this new ministry of state. For example, while I see the Prime Minister has corrected himself, or left the door open to correction, in his remarks today, the Department of Agriculture is not one of the resource-related departments which will be co-ordinated by the super ministry, nor is the Department of Fisheries. In other words, to the Trudeau government agriculture is no longer a resource for Canada, nor is fisheries a resource for Canada. In a country like Canada you simply cannot have a national industrial policy designed to encourage the development of our farm resources without taking account of the tremendous potential for growth in the country in the fields of agriculture, fisheries and forestry.

We are faced with the question as to exactly what is left in the place of these formerly important ministers which have now had their status downgraded. What exactly are the powers of this new super minister? What can he initiate? What can his officials initiate? What can they stop? What is their power independent of other ministers in the cabinet? What exactly are they there for?
These are questions which 1 am sure the minister himself will try to answer, but I must say that on the record of this government, our view as to what they are trying to do with this new super ministry is quite simply this: They are trying to fool the Canadian people. They are trying to pretend there is now a new seriousness about economic policy and economic problems in the country, and they are putting together a structure which will look good and do very little.
We in this party, committed as we are to the view that there must be significant structural reforms if responsible members of the government and of parliament are to be able to influence national policy in this country, think we are not receiving that kind of proposal today. We think that what we are receiving today is simply a smokescreen, simply another gimmick by a government that has excelled in gimmicks; and we think there is no major new power that will be assigned to this minister. We think he will have no power to start important things, no power to stop important things, and that his job is simply to be the freshest in a round of soothing faces that the Government of Canada put forth to a community concerned about the failure of economic policy.
What has happened here is that late in its life-indeed, in the first year of its afterlife, its fifth year in office-this government has recognized that it will not be able to survive another election without an economic policy. That was the reason the election was delayed. That was the reason we had the sermon from on high on August 1. The government knew that it could no longer get away with ignoring fundamental economic problems in the country. But true to form, instead of responding to these problems, instead of going to their root, instead of bringing in budgets that might have stimulated growth in the country, instead of starting on a serious exercise of getting the provinces together and getting the other partners in the community together to work toward common economic goals, this government resorted to a series of gimmicks. They
Economic Development
brought in a street fighter as Minister of Finance and that was going to solve everything. It has not.
Since the government was not able to change the Minister of Finance again, it came up with another gimmick which it hopes will persuade Canadians that the government is serious about economic development. The government can indicate that of course it is serious, that it has a new minister. But, there are serious questions as to which responsibilities of other ministers this minister will take, and what he will do with them. That is not his most basic problem. It is that he is supposed to co-ordinate economic policy, and the government has no economic policy to co-ordinate.

Mr. Speaker, the new minister across the chamber is politely indicating that he will be right back. I appreciate his consideration, because my comments will deal with the subject we are supposed to be dealing with today, namely, economic planning. If ever we needed a demonstration of the problems with our economy, we received one today from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). He came in from a flight from Paris and rambled on for approximately 20 minutes. His speech was an abbreviated version of the one which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) made some weeks ago. I wish he had taken a longer flight and skipped the entire debate.
Then we heard from the official opposition. 1 listened with great care for an indication whether they were for or against planning, but I did not hear one. It appears the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) is in favour of "significant structural reform." If this debate was taking place in any other industrial country of the world, such as Norway, France or Japan, whether social democratic governments or not, it would have been laughed at. The hon. Leader of the Opposition is going to Japan. I hope when he returns that he will feel free to talk about economic planning. Japan is one society which talks about it and does it.
First I should like to deal with the problems in general and specific terms, and then I should like to deal with some workable solutions to those problems. We have had ten years

of the Prime Minister. If we have ever had an admission of failure in terms of national economic policy, it was today when the Prime Minister indicated the need for the proposed planning mechanism. After ten years, the number of unemployed in Canada has tripled; inflation has risen by 100 per cent; income distribution between regions in Canada and individuals within regions has worsened; the rich have become relatively richer and the poor relatively poorer; and there is a problem which is central to our economy, that is, an increase in the degree of foreign ownership in the manufacturing sector, the core sector for an advanced economy. This has increased, not lessened, in the past ten years. These are the significant ten-year old developmental problems associated with the government.
At one point in his speech, the Prime Minister said that it is time to take the next step. He should have taken that step ten years ago. He should have made a commitment ten years ago to deal with economic planning in a manner which would have ameliorated the problems of income distribution, unemployment, inflation and foreign ownership in the manufacturing sector of our economy. In all of those categories, the situation has worsened in the past decade, not improved.
Not only is the need to create this new department an admission of failure of the long run during the past decade, but it is a significant failure also in the short run. This was recognized by the Minister of Finance who brought in three budgets. There is a lower growth rate in our economy than was promised as recently as last August, when the Prime Minister had a new vision after the summit meeting in Bonn. The three budgets have not improved the degree of economic performance in the economy. Monthly the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) witnesses the continuing imbalance in trade in manufacturing products between our country and others. This should be a central concern of economic policy.
There is a need for planning in an industrially advanced economy such as ours, and I will attempt to make some suggestions in this regard. Before doing so, I should like to refer to the tacit admission of the failure of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion which in recent years has seen the problems of regional development worsening rather than improving. The economically advanced areas of the country have made more progress, while areas in Atlantic Canada and the province of Quebec have fallen behind.
There have been both short-run and long-run failures which have been acknowledged by the need, at long last, to create a new instrument for planning. The particular mechanism being proposed, is it good or bad? Surely that question should enter this debate at some point. It is relevant to consider whether what is being proposed will work in our economy. To put it euphemistically, the Minister of Finance, the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers (Mr. Andras) and the Prime Minister have conflicting views as to what this new entity is all about.
The government chose to name the former president of the treasury board the new President of the Board of Economic

Development Ministers. That significant phrase came right out of the corporate experience of the government. Initially the Prime Minister said that this new entity would deal with macro and micro economic policy. He made this distinction. The Minister of Finance was to deal with one, and the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers was to deal with the other. Perhaps it was the first time in Canadian history that a minister of finance indicated that he was not sure of the difference between micro and macro, that everyone believed that he was telling the truth. The Prime Minister gave one description. A number of ministers have interpreted the purpose of the board entirely differently from the Prime Minister. What will happen to the old cabinet committee on economic policy? Will it remain in existence? Will it remain unused, as has been the case in the past decade? Surely if we are talking about a planning board or instrument, some discussion is relevant concerning the priorities. Certainly this would be true in any industrially advanced country.
What will the board do? The new President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers indicated that he believed it would be a one-stop shopping service for business looking for government support.

The Department of Finance has been a one-stop shopping service for years for corporate handouts which have been unrelated to specific economic performance. He left every implication that he really did not see planning as being relevant at all. The implication he left with me, at least, was that all the government could do was get out of the private sector's way. In some areas that is entirely appropriate, but anyone should know, and I am sure the new president of the board does, that in a modern market economy that is scarcely enough, and there are a number of positive things that a government must do. Some leadership in directing the economy is required. He has downplayed the whole planning role and suggested it is essentially going to be a negative instrument to get out of the private sector's way.
The Minister of Finance in his budget speech went out of his way to say that in a market society planning was probably inappropriate. That statement was specifically in his speech and surely could not have been accidental. Again this is a point that would not be made in any other industrial country. No other industrial country would have the government party and the official opposition somehow saying that in the 1980s, nearly into the twenty-first century, it was inappropriate in a market economy to have planning. That boggles the mind, Mr. Speaker.
The government neglected in the terms of reference for this board to make any reference to the problems of Canadian women. Regional problems are referred to, quite appropriately. Problems in respect of income equality between individuals is referred to and that is entirely appropriate. But where is
December 13, 1978

reference to that other great dimension of inequality that is still with us in this country in this century, and that is equality of the sexes? Is there any reference there at all? I suggest there is not. This is not merely an academic point.
The government of the United States, to its credit, has established affirmative action programs embodied in legislation which have become the central concern of that government in the United States in respect of economic areas for women. There is nothing, I repeat, nothing, in the mandate given to this new board which deals with that other central inequality in our country which surely should be a leading concern of politicians at every level.
Perhaps the most important structural point I want to make about this board, and I say this candidly, is that a similar mechanism was tried by the Labour party in Great Britain and it failed. Harold Wilson, when he was prime minister early in the 1960s, set up within the cabinet structure in England a planning mechanism which sounds almost identical to the one that has now been established by the Government of Canada. About four years later Mr. Wilson abolished it because it did not work.
Let me say something about why it did not work because it is central to my understanding of whether the government is really serious about what it is doing. In Great Britain it was abolished by Harold Wilson, according to George Brown, the former minister of the Crown who had responsibilities similar to those now taken on by the new president of the board here-

Yes, I have read the Crossman diaries and some other information that goes with them. It was abolished because, according to what comes out in the Crossman diaries and what comes out of the published statements by George Brown, who was a minister, that minister was not given overriding authority in respect of economic policy. There was continual confrontation and conflict between the minister of finance, or the chancellor of the exchequer in the British system, and the man who was supposed to be responsible for planning.
If you look at these terms of reference, and if you look at the order in council that was passed to set up this new department, you will get no indication at all that there is a recognition of the problem that is to be faced by the Government of Canada. Quite obviously conflict remains. The responsibilities of the Minister of Finance have not been changed. The president of the board now has some over-all general policy for some kind of economic development, but when there is a conflict how is it to be resolved? Surely if the government were serious about economic planning it would have to give the new ministry precedence over the ministry of finance, and that should have been spelled out in the order in council setting up the department.
Economic planning should have an overriding priority, and if there is a conflict between the Ministry of Finance and the ministry of planning, planning should have the priority, par-
Economic Development
ticularly if that is to be the leading concern in the country. However, that is not the case here. I repeat, we are establishing a planning mechanism which even on paper has been demonstrated in the experience of the government of Great Britain to be a failure in practice.
This leads me to my conclusion, and that is that the Government of Canada is not any more serious about planning now than it has been in the past. The Minister of Finance has to be taken as indicating the true direction of the government when he said in his budget address that the Government of Canada really did not believe in planning in a market economy; and the new president of the board has to be taken seriously when he said that really what this new agency is going to do is provide a one-stop service to the private sector in relation to some kind of handouts or the removal of red tape. I would repeat that the removal of red tape is desirable in many aspects of the government's relationship with the private sector. I would also repeat that that cannot be the centra! purpose of the new planning board.
My colleagues and I see the creation of this new instrument as simply one more public relations gesture by a government that has recognized at long last that its unpopularity is due in the main to its failure to come to grips with the Canadian economy, to deal with regional inequalities, to deal with income inequalities between individuals and to deal with inequalities between the sexes. That is why this government is unpopular. Instead of coming to grips with these problems in a serious way by setting up a serious planning instrument, this government has taken over a program that failed in Great Britain, that was recognized as a failure and abandoned by that government. It is now attempting through public relations to convince the people of Canada before the next election that it takes economic problems seriously. We just do not believe that.
Let me briefly say something about why we think it is important to plan in an economy, particularly in the context of the problems we are facing in our land at this time. I want to indicate first of all that the planning we have in mind is not simply intervention in the economy. We have always had intervention. Let me say to my colleagues in the Tory party that I wish they would read some Canadian history. If they did they would recognize, for example, that unlike the United States we have always had more government intervention in our economy than they have, by a long shot. In fact, if this country had relied simply on market principles it would not have come into existence.
The first government of Sir John A. Macdonald recognized that something called "national policy" was necessary at one point. He recognized that when you have regions as disparate as Atlantic Canada, the west coast, the prairies and Ontario, with the tremendous market forces at bay to the south of us in the United States, government intervention would always be required in our economy at a much higher level than in the United States.
It is not merely intervention that is needed, because all too often that simply means something negative-buying up rail-

ways and creating the CPR at the expense of one generation, or bailing out the aircraft industry again at the expense of another generation. Planning as it has been demonstrated to exist in other countries of the world, and as we see it performing here, has one essential purpose, and that is to take steps now to create something better down the road. Economic planning is central to dealing with the great inequalities that exist between individuals, regions and sexes. It makes sense, particularly in a land like ours, to have a very sophisticated instrument of planning, and perhaps the most sophisticated in the world will be necessary to do the job that is required in our land.
We want further planning, not for its own sake, not to give some bureaucrat or academic the vicarious pleasure of seing an idea worked out, but because it is essentially a human device for human purposes. In this context Sweden, Belgium, Norway, France, Japan and West Germany have four or five-year economic plans with regular submissions to their parliaments. When a government is formed in one of those countries, one of the central tasks it has is to come before the legislature with the economic development plan for the next four or five years, which becomes the central matter for debate on both sides of the House. I wish the other national parties in this country would accept that idea and come before parliament with a plan on which we could have meaningful debate, instead of trivial, nitpicking matters such as whether some bureaucrat is taking another bureaucrat's function or whether a ministry is being removed which ought to be continued in operation. Such debate is most trivial.
What are some of the concrete problems facing us in 1978 and how do we propose to deal with them? The first issue is regional inequality. We believe that it is not right for central Canada, Alberta and British Columbia to see our fellow Canadians in Atlantic Canada and the eastern townships in Quebec dependent on some form of hand-out. It is an illusion to believe that the private sector will remove the difficulties which exist in these areas.

If we are going to come to grips with the problems in Atlantic Canada, then we have to do what other countries have done and move in with public capital and long range plans. Why is it inappropriate for the Government of Canada to borrow money for development when it is entirely appropriate for Bell Canada or other huge conglomerates to borrow capital and pay interest on it for the same purpose? Government development through public sector investment can be just as effective financially in the long run, and more so when we are dealing with regional inequality, as in the private sector.
There is in Cape Breton the potential for serious long-range development. Instead of having 30 per cent unemployment, or

unemployment ad infinitum, and being dependent on handouts which they do not want, they could be financially independent. There are many people on that island who are trained in the steel industry and mining industry. Capital should be invested to build the most modern steel facility in the world for that area. I know that the market situation for steel in the world is tight at the moment, and it may mean for the next year or so that the operation would run at a loss. But I repeat a point I have made in this House before. General Motors does not plan for six months down the road; it plans for six years and, indeed, six decades down the road. It is time we started doing the same thing at the national level. The only way this can be done with federal funds, because Nova Scotia certainly does not have the funds. Such an investment would put that part of Cape Breton on a creative, economic basis on which it could start contributing to the rest of Canada. 1 am sure that Cape Bretoners would like that much more than the rest of us.
