The hon. member has made some critical observations. 1 was in that part of the country recently and was told by the fishermen that instead of using the opportunities provided by an 85-cent dollar to expand our markets in Europe and the United States, they are simply taking in higher profits. That short-run perspective of the business sector is just the opposite to what the Japanese have done. The private sector in Japan has at least had the sense to take lower profits in the short run so that they would expand in the markets and grow in the future. We should be doing this kind of thing in Atlantic Canada with government initiative and imagination.
In recent months new investment has come to the west coast from Japan. They have begun to provide financial assistance to people in our fishing industry on the west coast because those people could not get that financial assistance from the Government of Canada, their own provincial government or the banks of Canada. Japanese investors have come in with better terms, and in exchange are tying that aid to long-range market commitments in Japan.
While it may be beneficial in the short run for fishermen to get a good price right now, they are being locked into long-range commitments to sell fish at a price down the road which may not be advantageous to Canadian fishermen. Another factor is that the Japanese are receiving the fish in bulk and having the processing done in Japan for re-export. Instead of having a developmental policy on our west coast which would not force our fishermen into such long-range commitments, and instead of having a developmental policy which would have the fish processing plants in Canada rather than Japan, we have allowed and we are allowing continuing inroads by a foreign country into a major sector involving Canadian resources.
This kind of imaginative use of federal capital which would take substantial amounts invested in the short run for long-range benefits is what is required. We did it once with the railways of this country. There were a lot of mistakes and give-aways and that ought not to be repeated. But there was a time when we had a long-range perspective in mind in building this country. It is time we had that perspective in terms of industrial development.
The second area of concern is the manufacturing industry. In that context the economic tragedy is of such proportions that one does not quite know where to begin. There are countries in Europe with much smaller populations than ours that have a durable and creative manufacturing base, independently owned. There are countries like Sweden with economic, geographical problems, thousands of miles in length, very diverse, wintery conditions and small markets that have managed to do about 1,000 per cent better than we have in developing their own manufacturing industry. The reality is that we have relied too long on the excuse of a small market in Canada and difficult geographical circumstances. These are just excuses for inaction.
Economic Development
The fundamental decision that was made in this regard in my lifetime, and the decision that has to be reversed, is one associated with the name C. D. Howe and with the Liberals of that time. Some two decades ago they decided that because of our small population this country ought to survive by selling off our resources and we would buy back finished products. It was thought we would have the net benefit because there would always be a shortage of resources and it was argued that other countries, particularly the United States, could produce goods at a lower cost because of their larger populations.
The chickens came home to roost, Mr. Speaker. We are discovering that third world countries such as Venezuela, Mexico, Indo-China and others have resources that we thought were unique to Canada. Instead of cornering the world market on nickel, copper and other minerals, we are facing competition from the third world for resources. As a result we have big lay-offs by companies like Inco in Thompson, in British Columbia and in dozens of other communities. We can no longer rely on selling off our resources as the key to prosperity even if it made sense, and for many reasons it does not.
Since the time of C. D. Howe the industry of western Europe has modernized and has become sophisticated. Japanese industry has also modernized and as the people of Quebec know very well, third world countries are producing shoes and textiles of a sophisticated type. We have lost out on both grounds.
The domestic manufacturing industry, which was set up simply to service Canadian markets and not to go after exports, has to compete with a modern Europe and modernized third world countries in manufacturing. The resources that we have wanted to export as a source of prosperity are having to meet competition from third world countries.
We have to deal with this problem on a long-range basis, Mr. Speaker, and I was hoping to see some commitment to that effect by the government. We have to deal with the problem of foreign ownership. It is not a matter of blaming the United States or Germany or The Netherlands for investment; it is a matter of recognizing who is to set our priorities. Is it to be people in other countries or are we to do it ourselves?
At this moment in Canada there are some 100 large companies which control more than 50 per cent of our manufacturing, mining and forestry industries. Of these, two-thirds are owned and controlled outside Canada. The result is that in 50 per cent of the business area there are companies that do not conduct their own research and development, companies that do not pursue exports because their parent firms in the United States or abroad do that. There are companies that do not innovate because, in the main, the parent firms do the innovation.
As long as we leave that structure intact, as long as we leave foreign control of our major manufacturing sector as the characteristic form of manufacturing in Canada, just so long will we remain in immense difficulty in regard to manufacturing.

December 13, 1978
Economic Development
The fundamental question for Canadians is: Who is running our country? Who is setting our priorities? Is it to be Gulf Oil, is it to be Phillips, is it to be Ford, is it to be IBM, or is it, for once, to be Canadians? Are we at long last to come to grips with this problem as other industrial countries have? I say on behalf of my colleagues that this kind of action is long overdue.
I should like to put on record some aspects of the economic development policy that we are advocating. First of all, we say that we in Canada should do as the Japanese did and as most industrial countries in western Europe have done, and as the United States did for most of the nineteenth century; we should ensure that most Canadian needs are met by Canadian production. We must restructure the Canadian economy to ensure that most Canadian consumer dollars are spent on goods and services produced in Canada.
Two or three ideas are central to the implementation of this proposal, not because they are dreamed up in some abstract way but because they have worked in other countries. We should realize where people are spending their money. It is known that 80 per cent to 85 per cent of Canadian disposable income is spent on housing, transportation and food. We should concentrate on these sectors. We should make sure we have the best housing industry in the world that could lead to exports in that field, and we should make sure that everything that goes into a house in this country is produced in this country.
In the transportation sector we should make sure that what goes into it is produced in Canada.
We should ensure that most of our food is produced in Canada. Agriculture associations meeting in this city in recent weeks and months have stated self-sufficiency in food as a Canadian goal. The New Democratic Party believes in that for the sake of security for Canadian farmers and as a Canadian economic objective. The more food we produce in Canada, the less we buy abroad and the fewer dollars we send out of the country. That makes good economic sense.
We should specialize in certain key sectors of industry. We should do what other industrialized countries have done and not spread all our economic investment over different sectors, but instead concentrate on the agricultural implements business, for example, and on food processing and equipment. Good economic arguments can be made for saying that they are key sectors in which Canadians already have some leadership in world terms which, if developed further, would lead to access to export markets, and this is very important.
Central to all of this has to be a major shift in resource policy. We as a people should be exporting steel products, not iron ore. We as a people should be exporting furniture and paper, not raw pulp and unprocessed paper. We should be exporting plastics and petro-chemical products, not unrefined gas and oil.
This is the central concern of my party for the development of Canada in the future. We must at long last recognize that

Canadian resources ought to be developed by Canadians primarily for the benefit of Canadians. That has to be a central economic concern. We must stop exporting our fish to Japan and buying back the finished product. We must stop exporting so much lumber to the United States and buying back the finished product. We must at long last begin exporting finished goods and not raw resources.
There are a variety of instruments to implement these objectives. In my remaining time I want to indicate how these goals could be achieved. The central reason that we have not done this before has nothing to do with our proximity to the United States or to geographic difficulties, or indeed with the cultural tensions we have experienced from time to time. It has everything to do with the lack of political will. That has been the central problem in this country.
There are a number of instruments we can use that have been developed by other countries which have worked well. One is tariffs. We must be very concerned now that we are moving from a high tariff country with no planning to a low tariff country with no planning. That seems to be the general drift of the GATT negotiations. In certain sectors we may have to create-

I appreciate the consideration of other members and I will try to be brief. We must use our tariff policy, but not in a mindless way. In changing tariffs we must, as other countries have done, build in in certain sectors non-tariff barriers so that we can preserve certain sectors now, and indeed lay the foundation for broader and more long-range growth in those sectors in the future. We must not simply phase them out, which seems to be the current inclination of the government.
With respect to purchasing policy, Mr. Speaker, in the United States for years they have had a policy in which something like 30 per cent of the purchases of the federal government had to be from small businesses. That happens to make good economic sense. Unlike large firms, most small businessmen do indeed compete and innovate and create more jobs.
We could have a purchasing policy like that in Canada where there is a commitment on the part of the national government to buy, say, 30 per cent of all their requirements from small businesses. Small businesses are almost uniformly owned by Canadians. They are not owned and controlled outside our borders.
Another instrument is the use of planning agreements. Planning agreements have worked very well in Holland, Great Britain, France, Belgium, Sweden and Norway. In these countries a specific set of tax policies is negotiated with major firms over a five-year period. In this way the firms know where they
December 13, 1978

stand and know that tax policy will not change from one year to the next. The private sector must be aware of that information. In return for specfic tax concessions, specific benefits would accrue in terms of creation of jobs, research and development and export commitments. Planning agreements are something that have worked well in other countries and ought to be duplicated here.
Another instrument we have advocated is the establishment of a Canadian investment fund. I could speak at great length about this, but 1 simply want to make the point that it has worked well in Sweden where a special tax is levied on large companies. If companies put money into this fund, they do not pay tax on that part of the revenue. The government then plans where that fund could be used best to stimulate new development, and then the private company from which the revenue was originally derived would ultimately receive a benefit. The important thing is that this could be an instrument of the government to make sure that development occurs in certain areas and in sectors that need it.
Second, in terms of the cyclical nature of the economy, in Sweden this method is used most effectively in stimulating the economy. The level of investment can be controlled in terms of timing as well.
Finally, as I said earlier, we say that certain key sectors which have a particular potential for export should be concentrated on for development. 1 repeat that planning is not something new. It is not something that did not work in other countries, and it is not a panacea. A commitment to planning now will not remove all our difficulties overnight.
In conclusion, planning in a modern economy has been undertaken in other countries and it has worked very well. On behalf of my colleagues in this House I say that it is time we planned. It is time that we made our decisions. It is time we shaped our future. It is time that Canadians controlled Canada.

First of all, at the provincial level, then at the level of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, and finally by the board for economic expansion.

The government seems surprised to hear the cry of the provinces against the central government.
The motion introduced today, Mr. Speaker, is a perfect example of the dictatorial behaviour of this government. But when we examine the formation of the Ministry of State for Economic Development we realize that that super-ministry will be a perfect instrument of centralization to further control natural resources and agriculture in every province which have been asking for the patriation of their jurisdictions in those areas.
We can thus see a duplication of departments in all sectors to the economy-forestry, mining, fisheries, regional economic expansion, energy in its various forms, science and technology, agriculture and food industry, and so on. A new department was created a few years ago, the Department of Amateur Sport. How is it that the government has so much money that it can-afford duplicating departments which already exists in the provinces? A little while ago I contacted the Minister of Amateur Sport in order to get a grant for our region, which this year will host a national curling match, so as to make this a success like in all other provinces. And every time I contacted this minister I received the same reply: no funds available for grants to regions or provinces.
The money was allocated to the Canadian Amateur Sport Federation. The government went to see the Amateur Sport Federation and distributed the money to the provinces. What it did, Mr. Speaker, was to appoint a minister to collect the money and send it to the federation just like it was done for many years. I believe we have reach a point where we may well wonder whether the Canadian government has too much money to do what it did in the past.

I would firstly indicate that 1 support the motion as strongly as 1 can. Time has come in Canada to set up a process ensuring better co-ordination and cohesion in our economic development programs and policies.
I would like at this point to draw a distinction which apparently escaped the attention of a number of people who commented on the Prime Minister's announcement at the end of November last and his resolution tabled on December 4. 1 noted this afternoon the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broad-bent), the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby also made the same error. I wish the hon. member had also told his leader that he should have spoken about the resolution instead of the phony things he spoke about which have nothing to do with the resolution before us.
The Leader of the Opposition said that DREE has been ineffective and has been undercut because other departments have done what DREE has been doing. What the government is doing by the establishment of the Economic Development Board, after eight or nine years of experience with DREE, at a time of very rapid economic growth in Canada, and now that we have serious adjustments to make, is to refine the means and the tools for the economic development of the country. This board will bring about better co-ordination and cohesion and will ensure that economic development programs of the federal government are more effective when we are not in a
period of rapid growth, when we have to make serious economic adjustments, when we have to decide, because of the new economic context, what exactly will be the role of the government and what kind of society we want to organize. It becomes more important now to assure ourselves that the tools of the government are more efficient. This board does not reduce the influence of the other departments.
The role of the Minister of Finance is to deal with monetary matters, taxation matters and economic policy. The Leader of the Opposition does not know the difference between economic policy and economic development programs. There is a large difference between them. He said this afternoon that the country's economic policy will be impaired because we will have better means of making sure that economic development programs work better. Does he mean he would not have economic development programs and he would leave everything to macroeconomics? Does he wish us to believe that in the enunciation of a budget, which is one statement of economic policy, one can deal with all possible problems in terms of economic development programs? That is a complete fallacy; there is no way you can do that.
The Leader of the Opposition mentioned the role of the Treasury Board. I hope that the new board will not be a board exactly like the Treasury Board which, by its very nature, must be a regressive institution because it must ensure that all programs and initiatives stay within a certain fiscal context. The job of the Treasury Board is to put on the brakes. The role of this economic board is one of a positive agent. It is to make sure that things are done, not like the Treasury Board which makes sure that things remain within the fiscal context which has been set by the economic policy. That is the basic difference between the two boards, and I am glad to see that the government makes that difference.
In Canada we have in one part of the country, in the west, great opportunities in terms of economic development, and in the east the economy lags. However, I would just like to point out that the challenge in both cases is exactly the same. When things go well, as they do in western Canada and in the north, when we have an opportunity to do things, the challenge is to ensure that the organization of society will be such that what you want will happen. In areas which need assistance, the challenge is there also. The challenge is the same whether there is too much development or not enough development. I am glad to see that at this time in our economic history we will have this kind of co-ordination in our economic programs at the federal level.
